introduction.p: An optimization problem asks for a maximum or minimum under given constraints. First choose variables, determine their allowed values, and express the quantity to be optimized as a function. Then use derivatives and endpoint checks to compare all relevant candidates.

exercise.title: Why is the first task of optimization translation, not calculus?

statement.p: A real question arrives as a sentence about a box, a fence, or a can, not as maximize f(x). In your own words, why must we first name the objective, the constraint, and the domain, and why is that translation already most of the mathematics?

example.title: the shortest reflected path
example.p: A point A is located a units above a straight mirror, and a point B is located b units above the same mirror. Their horizontal separation is L. A light ray travels from A to the mirror and then to B. Where should it hit the mirror to make the total distance as small as possible?

Here a,b,L>0. The second derivative is D''(x)=a^2/(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}+b^2/((L-x)^2+b^2)^{3/2}>0, and the critical point lies in (0,L), so it is the unique absolute minimum. This condition is the familiar reflection rule: the incoming and outgoing angles are equal. The derivative has found the law of reflection from a shortest-path principle.

subsection.title: Endpoint checks and physical feasibility
subsection.p: Optimization problems are not finished when we find a critical number.
A critical number is a candidate. It may give a maximum, a minimum, neither, or it may not be physically allowed.
The correct conclusion depends on the domain.

But endpoints do not always lose. If a problem asks for a minimum, an endpoint may win. If a domain is open, the best value may not be attained at all. If a critical point lies outside the physical domain, it is irrelevant.

note.title: The domain is part of the problem
note.p: A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. The domain tells the formula which choices are allowed.

paragraphs.p: Related rates asked how fast quantities change together. Optimization asked which choice is best. Both depended on building a model and then reading a derivative.

But real measurements are rarely exact. A radius may be 3 cm only to the nearest millimeter. A length may have a small error. The next question is not the best exact choice, but how sensitive an answer is to small changes.

exercise.title: Why is the domain part of the problem, not an afterthought?

statement.p: A critical number may give a max, a min, neither, or a value that is not physically allowed. In your own words, why must we check endpoints and feasibility, and why can the derivative find the best point for the wrong domain?

hint.p: A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. Endpoints can win, and a critical point outside the allowed interval is irrelevant.
